title: Sita's argument
hook: Rama asks Sita to stay behind, and she makes her case

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm toward blame. This is daiva, he said: no blame for anyone. A new week begins, and Sita speaks.

Rama comes home with his news, and with a plan for Sita. She'll stay in Ayodhya and wait for him. He has thought it through, kindly, carefully, and alone. In Valmiki's telling, Sita is many things in this scene, and quiet isn't the first of them. She hears the whole plan out. Then, piece by piece, she takes it apart.
screen: `RAMA'S PLAN FOR SITA.` → `KINDLY, CAREFULLY, ALONE.` → `SHE TAKES THE PLAN APART.`

segments.voice: Sita has been waiting at home for the procession. She sees Rama come in alone and pale, with no royal umbrella and no music, and she knows something's wrong. He tells her everything, then gives instructions. Stay here. Serve my father and my mothers. Don't praise me in front of Bharata; men in power don't like hearing others praised. Keep your vows, live simply, and wait for me. Valmiki says Sita answers out of love and anger together. Her first point is sharp. Father, mother, brother, son: each lives out their own fortune. But a wife shares her husband's. If you've been sent to the forest, so have I. Her second is practical. If you go today, I'll walk ahead of you, trampling the thorns and sharp grass so your path is easier. Her third is about what she wants. She'd rather be in the forest with him than in a palace without him. She isn't asking permission to suffer. She describes the forest as a place she wants to see: the mountains, the lakes, the lotus ponds, the birds. She'll be happy there, she says, as long as he's there. Notice the shape of it. Rama made a decision for both of them, kindly and alone. Sita refuses to be decided for. Valmiki gives her room to say so, at length, in her own voice, and she isn't finished yet.
screen: `NO UMBRELLA, NO MUSIC.` · `RAMA'S PLAN: STAY HERE.` · `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S FORTUNE.` · `I'LL WALK AHEAD, TRAMPLING THORNS.` · then, large: `SITA REFUSES TO BE DECIDED FOR.`

segments.voice: Think of a decision someone made for you out of kindness, without asking, and one you've made for someone else the same way. Let both sit side by side. On each breath out, imagine handing the question back, open, so the other person can answer it in their own voice.
Sita's argument. Asked to stay behind, she answers out of love and anger: a wife shares her husband's fortune, and she'll walk ahead of him through the thorns.
Your line: I'll walk ahead, trampling thorns. Rama has one more try in him. Day five hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Sita is honored in Hindu devotion as Rama's companion, and in this scene the text gives the choice to share his exile to her, in her own voice.

original.note: Sanskrit sītā: a furrow. her name recalls how Janaka found her in a plowed field.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita simply followed Rama.
what it means: Rama tells her to stay, and she argues him out of it.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki says Sita speaks out of love and anger together, and gives her a long speech of her own, with more to come in the next chapters.

chat.says: Why did Sita want to go to the forest? Couldn't she wait safely at home?
options: A wife shares her husband's fortune, she said, and she'd be happy wherever he was.
She was afraid Kaikeyi would harm her if she stayed behind in the palace.
Rama ordered her to come along, and she didn't dare refuse him.
chat.meaning: Sita argues that a wife shares her husband's fortune, and she'd rather be in the forest with Rama than a palace without him.

Ayodhya.meaning: Rama's home city, capital of Kosala

Valmiki.meaning: the poet-sage who composed the Ramayana

recall: Kaikeyi's maid, who turned joy to fear

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 26 (Rama tells Sita; asks her to stay)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
'Love and anger together' renders praṇayakopa or similar in the text; confirm.
Trapdoor claim 'one of the longest stretches of a woman's voice in the epic' is a reading, not a count; a Keeper may soften it.
